Key distinguishing features include morphology (e.g., ulceration, scaling, induration, color change), growth pattern, and risk factors. Since the lesion is painless and chronic, malignancy must be ruled out. The next critical step is to characterize the lesion visually and clinically — size, color, surface features (e.g., ulcerated, crusted, verrucous, smooth), borders, and consistency — which requires direct observation. These dramatically increase the risk of actinic cheilitis and its progression to invasive SCC — the most common malignancy of the lower lip. The lesion’s painless, persistent (3-month) course further aligns with early SCC, which often lacks symptoms until advanced. While benign lesions (e.g., fibroma) can occur in smokers, they rarely persist unchanged for months without trauma-related fluctuation; moreover, chronic sun exposure makes actinic damage far more likely. Given the high-risk profile, the next critical step is direct tissue evaluation. Clinical impression alone is insufficient — biopsy is the gold standard to confirm or exclude dysplasia or malignancy. A simple, office-based incisional or shave biopsy of the lesion is indicated and will provide definitive histopathologic diagnosis.

Keratin pearls are pathognomonic for well-to-moderately differentiated SCC, and dysplasia confirms malignant transformation. Given the location (lower lip), chronic sun exposure, tobacco use, and painless persistent lesion, this fits the most common presentation of cutaneous/oral SCC. No further diagnostic testing is needed to establish the diagnosis — the histopathology is confirmatory. The task is to identify the single most likely diagnosis, and all evidence converges unequivocally on squamous cell carcinoma.

[DIAGNOSIS] Squamous cell carcinoma
